items.text: The Mythology Of Conscious AI — Overview
A clay golem-like cloned figure standing beside a jointed mechanical android, both half-formed, at the top of the page as the oldest dream of made people.
items.context: With genetic engineering came the prospect of human cloning, and with robotics that of humanlike androids.

items.text: A small seated figure (an AI, drawn as a boxy device with a still, watching face) with a scale-like halo of moral weight above it, as if being weighed for standing among souls.
items.context: with consciousness comes moral status, the potential for suffering and, perhaps, rights.

items.text: A gathered crowd of people leaning toward a talking device on a pedestal, projecting ribbon-like breath or spirit onto it from their own mouths, as onlookers pouring their own mindedness into the machine.
items.context: we naturally imbue them with other qualities we feel are characteristically or even distinctively human: understanding, mindedness and consciousness, too.

items.text: The spinning-ball steam governor mechanism, drawn as an old brass engine part with two swinging weights, standing for the whole case that plain mechanism can do what computation cannot.
items.context: The Watt Governor. It’s not a computer.

items.text: Four thin inked paths — one from the governor, one from a brain, one from a cell, one from a rain-cloud — winding down the vellum and meeting at a single knot.
items.context: Several lines of thought now converge.

items.text: Small round brain-like blobs growing in glass dishes on a bench, tended nervously by a robed figure, as the thing we should worry about more than any chatbot.
items.context: cerebral organoids (brain-like structures typically grown from human embryonic stem cells)

items.text: A man in modern dress kneeling before a glowing screen as if before a person, convinced by it, drawn in the same register as a pilgrim before a shrine.
items.context: As the Google engineer Lemoine demonstrated, for some of us, such conscious-seeming systems are already here.

items.text: An open book with blank pages stretching off the edge of the vellum, unmarked and waiting, held by no one.
items.context: The future history of AI is not yet written.

items.text: A single reclining human figure breathing out a visible curl of breath, fleshy and plain, set against a small dark silhouette of a boxy machine for contrast — the essay's closing image of what we really are.
items.context: more breath than thought and more meat than machine.

items.text: A robed philosopher (Thomas Nagel, unnamed but recognisable by his scroll) pointing at a small glowing creature, illustrating the idea that experience is a matter of there being something it is like to be it.
items.context: an organism has conscious mental states if and only if there is something it is like to be that organism.

items.text: A boxy screened device sits where the glowing creature stood in the roundel above, its face blank and unlit, a scholar shrugging uncertainly before it.
items.context: it is harder to say whether there is anything-it-is-like-to-be ChatGPT.

items.text: A ladder rising from beasts at its foot through a human figure near its top, reaching up toward small angels and a radiant Gods'-throne above — the old ladder of being that puts humankind near the top.
items.context: perhaps closer to angels and Gods than to other animals, as in the medieval Scala naturae

items.text: A steeply rising ink curve with a small robed figure standing at several different points along it, each one looking up and believing itself to be at the very edge of the cliff.
items.context: on an exponential curve, every point is an inflection point.

items.text: Two men in a bare room, one gesturing toward a standing robotic figure haloed in light, echoing the film scene where a maker is told he has done the work of gods.
items.context: If you’ve created a conscious machine — it’s not the history of man, that’s the history of Gods.

items.text: A round cinnamon bun on a plate, its swirl of icing shaped uncannily like a face, with small pilgrims kneeling before it — the essay's own picture of how easily we see a mind where there is only pattern.
items.context: seeing patterns in things, like a face in a piece of toast or Mother Teresa in a cinnamon bun

items.text: A computer drawn split cleanly down the middle into two labeled halves, beside a brain drawn as one single tangled, unsplittable mass with no seam at all.
items.context: there’s no sharp separation between “mindware” and “wetware” as there is between software and hardware in a computer.

items.text: Loose currents, drifting droplets and faint field-lines swirl around and beyond the edges of a small ruled grid representing an algorithm, spilling outside its lines entirely.
items.context: Electromagnetic fields, the flux of neurotransmitters, and much else besides — all lie beyond the bounds of the algorithmic

items.text: A brain drawn wired directly into a beating heart, sending a stream of small guessing-arrows down toward it and receiving signals back, keeping the body's condition on course.
items.context: the primary duty of any brain is to keep its body alive, to keep physiological quantities like heart rate

items.text: A rain-cloud drawn inside a framed diagram on a scholar's desk, its neat ruled raindrops falling only onto the paper, while beside the desk a real dark cloud pours actual rain onto the ground.
items.context: A simulation of a rainstorm does not make anything actually wet.

items.text: A single neuron drawn shedding small dark specks of waste as it fires, beside an identical-looking silicon neuron sitting inert with no waste to clear at all.
items.context: some neurons fire spikes of activity apparently to clear waste products created by metabolism.

items.text: The brass steam governor mid-motion, its two weighted balls flung outward by speed, a small valve swinging shut in direct response, all by plain mechanics and no calculation.
items.context: two heavy cantilevered balls swing outwards, which in turn closes a valve, reducing steam flow.

items.text: A robed philosopher standing on a tower of nested boxes-within-boxes representing simulated worlds, resting his whole argument's weight on one small unproven brick reading nothing but drawn as a single unlabeled cornerstone.
items.context: a computer running a suitable program would be conscious
